case_analysis.focal_point: Whether AEDPA’s bar on relitigating claims in 28 U.S.C. §2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners’ second-or-successive motions under 28 U.S.C. §2255—and, relatedly, whether §2244(b)(3)(E) strips the Supreme Court of certiorari jurisdiction to review courts of appeals’ authorization decisions in such §2255 cases.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. §§ 2244(b)(1), 2244(b)(3)(E), and 2255 (including AEDPA’s second-or-successive regime, plus the limitations rule in §2255(f)(3) as discussed for policy/fairness).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Bowe argues that §2244(b)(1)—textually drafted to govern state-prisoner habeas petitions under §2254—should not be imported into the distinct federal-prisoner postconviction scheme in §2255; applying it to §2255 wrongly adds an extra, judge-made barrier beyond Congress’s carefully enumerated §2255(h) gatekeeping criteria, deepens a recognized circuit split, and can preclude review of meritorious claims based on later Supreme Court decisions. He also contends that if §2244(b)(3)(E) is read to bar certiorari review of §2255 authorization rulings, it would create an accountability gap where the Court cannot resolve the split through normal certiorari—an issue highlighted by prior statements (including Justice Kavanaugh’s in Avery and Justice Sotomayor/Justice Jackson’s statement in In re Bowe).
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States (and the court-appointed amicus defending the judgment below on Question 1) maintain that applying §2244(b)(1) to §2255 is consistent with AEDPA’s structure and finality goals: Congress intended robust restrictions on repeat litigation, and it is neither unfair nor unusual that even diligent federal prisoners may fail to benefit from intervening legal changes. They emphasize that AEDPA already accepts harsh timing/retroactivity consequences (e.g., §2255(f)(3) and Dodd show that prisoners can be time-barred from relying on new rights unless the Court makes them retroactive quickly), and that federal prisoners often have multiple prior opportunities (direct appeal, first §2255, etc.) before §2244(b)(1) matters. On jurisdiction, they invoke §2244(b)(3)(E)’s language to argue it forecloses Supreme Court certiorari review of authorization determinations, limiting review pathways.
key_precedents: Avery v. United States, 140 S. Ct. 1080 (2020) (statement respecting denial of certiorari by Justice Kavanaugh)
In re Bowe, 144 S. Ct. 1170 (2024) (statement respecting denial by Justice Sotomayor, joined by Justice Jackson)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s “integrated gatekeeping” reading of §2255(h)’s “certified as provided in section 2244” is the strongest respondent point, but under a minimalist, text-forward approach it still cannot overcome §2244(b)(1)’s express limitation to “an … application under section 2254”; treating the cross-reference as silently deleting that limitation is closer to amendment than interpretation. Justice Thomas’s structural concern about a serial-filing loophole identifies a plausible policy gap, yet AEDPA’s harshness (as in Dodd) cuts the other way: we enforce the obstacles Congress actually enacted, not add new ones to achieve symmetry. On jurisdiction, Justice Alito’s reliance on §2244(b)(3)(E)’s categorical phrasing is weighty, but Felker counsels against expanding review-stripping to foreclose certiorari over an antecedent question whether the court of appeals applied an inapplicable gatekeeping rule in the first place. A narrow disposition—§2244(b)(1) does not govern §2255 motions and (b)(3)(E) does not bar review of that threshold mismatch—best preserves institutional legitimacy without rewriting AEDPA.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s textual point—that §2244(b)(1) speaks only to “application[s] under section 2254” and we should not erase that limitation—is the strongest objection, but it does not overcome the original public meaning of §2255(h)’s command that a successive motion be “certified as provided in section 2244,” which incorporates the operative gatekeeping conditions defining what may be certified, not merely §2244(b)(3)’s filing mechanics. As Justice Barrett emphasizes, treating the cross-reference as a selective import invites an atextual cherry-pick that makes Congress’s linkage to §2244 largely performative and leaves a serial-relitigation gap inconsistent with AEDPA’s integrated scheme. On jurisdiction, I remain unpersuaded by the Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s proposed “antecedent error” carveout: §2244(b)(3)(E) categorically bars certiorari from the “grant or denial” of authorization, and Felker is better read (as Justice Alito notes) to enforce Congress’s channeling choice rather than to manufacture an exception not found in the text. Dodd’s acceptance of harsh AEDPA consequences reinforces that we must apply the statute’s enacted cross-references and review bars as written, not soften them by narrowing constructions driven by policy concerns.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s central objection—the express limitation in §2244(b)(1) to applications “under section 2254”—is serious, but it does not defeat the more natural reading of §2255(h)’s instruction that a successive motion be “certified as provided in section 2244,” which (as Justice Barrett explains) most sensibly incorporates the operative gatekeeping conditions that determine what is certifiable, not merely the filing mechanics in (b)(3). Treating the cross-reference as importing only (b)(3) invites the serial, repetitive authorization practice AEDPA was enacted to curb, creating an atextual asymmetry between state and federal prisoners that Congress avoided by welding §2255(h) to §2244’s framework. On jurisdiction, the petitioner side’s “antecedent error” carve-out (pressed by Roberts and Kagan) cannot be squared with §2244(b)(3)(E)’s categorical bar on certiorari from a “grant or denial” of authorization; Felker is better read, as Justice Thomas notes, to enforce that channeling choice rather than to license an exception the statute does not contain. Dodd’s acceptance of harsh consequences reinforces that we should not dilute AEDPA’s finality scheme by narrowing clear prohibitions or by construing cross-references to create loopholes.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s “integration” reading is the respondent side’s best point, but it still cannot overcome the explicit limiting text Congress chose: §2244(b)(1) applies only to “an application under section 2254,” and §2255(h)’s “certified as provided in section 2244” is naturally read, as the Chief Justice notes, to borrow the certification process in §2244(b)(3), not to silently erase (b)(1)’s §2254-only scope. Justice Kavanaugh’s “loophole” concern is a real structural worry, yet under a pragmatic, access-to-justice lens we should not add a categorical relitigation bar beyond §2255(h)’s enumerated gatekeeping criteria absent a clear statement—especially when later-recognized constitutional claims would bear the cost. On jurisdiction, Justice Thomas and Justice Alito emphasize §2244(b)(3)(E)’s categorical terms, but Felker’s caution against expansive readings of review-stripping supports the Chief’s and Justice Kagan’s narrower approach: certiorari is not barred where the court of appeals’ threshold mistake is applying an inapplicable gatekeeping rule. Dodd’s harshness shows AEDPA can be severe, but it does not justify making it harsher by judicially importing §2254-specific limits into §2255.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s “integrated gatekeeping framework” argument is the best case for Respondent, but under pragmatic textualism it still runs into the statute’s explicit boundary: §2244(b)(1) applies only to “an application under section 2254,” and §2255(h)’s “certified as provided in section 2244” cannot be read to silently delete that limiting clause without effectively amending the text. The structural worry about a serial-filing loophole is real, but Congress addressed federal prisoners in §2255(h) with enumerated criteria, and coherence favors treating the cross-reference as importing the certification mechanism in §2244(b)(3), not adding a new categorical claim bar keyed by §2254-only language. On jurisdiction, Justice Thomas’s and Justice Alito’s reliance on §2244(b)(3)(E)’s categorical bar is substantial, yet Felker (as the Chief notes) counsels against expanding review-stripping to foreclose certiorari over the antecedent legal question whether the court of appeals applied an inapplicable gatekeeping rule. I therefore remain with Petitioner on both the merits and a narrow reading of the certiorari bar that preserves workable Supreme Court supervision of AEDPA’s scheme.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s “integrated gatekeeping” reading is the strongest pushback: that “certified as provided in section 2244” incorporates the whole §2244(b) package, including (b)(1). But the Chief Justice is right that §2244(b)(1) is not a certification provision at all and, more importantly, it is expressly limited to “an application under section 2254”; under textualism we do not treat a cross-reference as silently deleting an express limitation Congress chose to include. Justice Thomas’s and Justice Alito’s structural/finality concerns may show Congress could have written a broader relitigation bar for §2255, but they cannot supply missing words—Dodd’s harsh-results lesson cuts the other way: we must apply AEDPA as enacted, not expand it for symmetry. On jurisdiction, I remain persuaded by Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s point that Felker counsels against reading §2244(b)(3)(E) to insulate from certiorari an antecedent legal error about whether the wrong gatekeeping rule was applied in the first place.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s textual point—that §2244(b)(1) by its terms applies only to an “application under section 2254”—is the hardest obstacle, and I take seriously his warning against treating that limitation as surplusage. But Justice Barrett’s reading better accounts for what §2255(h) actually does when it requires successive motions to be “certified as provided in section 2244”: that cross-reference most naturally incorporates the operative gatekeeping conditions that define what may be certified within §2244(b), not merely the (b)(3) mechanics, and otherwise creates an atextual carveout allowing repetitive authorization requests inconsistent with AEDPA’s integrated finality scheme. On jurisdiction, Justice Thomas’s and Justice Alito’s reliance on §2244(b)(3)(E)’s categorical bar is, in my view, more faithful to the text than the Chief’s Felker-based narrowing; Felker confirms Congress can channel Supreme Court review in this gatekeeping posture without our inventing an “antecedent error” exception. Nothing in the petitioner side’s arguments undermines that structural-textual reading enough to warrant switching votes, even if it is a close statutory fit problem.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s strongest point is that §2244(b)(1) expressly governs an “application under section 2254,” and we should hesitate to treat that limiting phrase as surplusage. But §2255(h) does not merely borrow §2244(b)(3)’s mechanics; it requires that a successive motion be “certified as provided in section 2244,” which, as Justice Thomas and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, most naturally incorporates the operative §2244(b) gatekeeping scheme defining what is certifiable, rather than inviting atextual cherry-picking of only one subsection. On jurisdiction, I remain unpersuaded by the Chief’s and Justice Kagan’s “antecedent legal error” carveout because §2244(b)(3)(E) categorically bars certiorari review of a “grant or denial” of authorization, and Felker is better read (with Justice Alito) as enforcing Congress’s channeling choice in this posture absent a constitutional problem. Nothing offered in conference genuinely undermines that integrated cross-reference reading under an original-public-meaning approach.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s “integrated gatekeeping” reading of §2255(h)’s “certified as provided in section 2244” is the most serious textual-structural case for Respondent, but it still requires treating a cross-reference as silently overriding §2244(b)(1)’s express limitation to “application[s] under section 2254,” effectively excising limiting language Congress chose to include. Justice Alito’s loophole concern has practical force, yet under a procedural-fairness and consequences lens it cannot justify importing a categorical relitigation bar into §2255(h) beyond the criteria Congress enumerated for federal prisoners—especially where later-arising Supreme Court decisions may be the only meaningful avenue to merits review. On jurisdiction, I am not persuaded by Justice Thomas’s categorical reading of §2244(b)(3)(E) because, as the Chief Justice argues, Felker supports construing review-stripping narrowly so it does not insulate an antecedent legal error about whether (b)(1) applies at all. Dodd’s acceptance of harsh AEDPA outcomes cautions against policy overrides, but here the narrower textual move is to enforce §2255(h) as written and treat §2244 as supplying the certification mechanism rather than adding §2254-specific substantive bars.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 2255(h) sets out Congress’s specific gatekeeping criteria for federal prisoners, and importing §2244(b)(1)’s relitigation bar—drafted for §2254 state-prisoner petitions—adds an extra restriction not textually anchored in §2255, contrary to a narrow, precedent-respecting approach to AEDPA’s carefully drawn scheme. On the jurisdiction question, §2244(b)(3)(E) should be read narrowly, consistent with the principle that limitations on this Court’s review are strictly construed, and with Felker v. Turpin’s recognition that AEDPA’s channeling of review did not eliminate the Court’s ability to exercise its essential functions. At minimum, where a court of appeals’ authorization ruling rests on a legally inapplicable gatekeeping requirement rather than a merits “grant or denial” within §2244(b)(3), the certiorari bar should not be extended to insulate that error from correction and to preserve institutional legitimacy. This path resolves the split on the statutory question while avoiding an unnecessarily broad construction of (b)(3)(E) that would impede the Court’s supervisory role.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The statutory text and structure of AEDPA indicate that Congress meant the court-of-appeals authorization regime in §2244(b)(3) to govern second-or-successive filings, and §2255(h) expressly incorporates that regime for federal prisoners; reading §2244(b)(1)’s relitigation bar to apply in this integrated scheme best accords with AEDPA’s evident aim of finality and limits on repetitive collateral attacks. Separately, §2244(b)(3)(E) states that the grant-or-denial of authorization “shall not be the subject of ... a petition for a writ of certiorari,” which is a clear jurisdiction-stripping directive that should be enforced as written. Felker v. Turpin confirms AEDPA’s restrictions on Supreme Court review can be applied according to their terms, while also recognizing that any residual constitutional questions do not justify disregarding unambiguous statutory limits. Whatever the policy consequences for later-arising claims, this Court has already enforced AEDPA’s harsh timing and retroactivity rules as written, see Dodd v. United States, and the remedy lies with Congress, not judicial revision.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: AEDPA’s structure indicates Congress meant stringent, uniform limits on repeat collateral attacks, and reading §2244(b)(1)’s relitigation bar to apply in the §2255 second-or-successive context best effectuates those finality and law-enforcement interests alongside §2255(h)’s gatekeeping criteria. The text of §2244(b)(3)(E)—that an authorization decision “shall not be the subject of a petition for rehearing or for a writ of certiorari”—is a clear jurisdictional withdrawal as to certiorari review of those threshold determinations, and we should not narrow it by judicial gloss. Felker v. Turpin supports honoring AEDPA’s channeling of review while recognizing the Court retained only its original-habeas authority there; it does not justify creating certiorari jurisdiction Congress expressly foreclosed. Dodd v. United States confirms that harsh timing/retroactivity consequences in §2255 are a feature Congress accepted, not a basis for expanding collateral review beyond the statute’s terms.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 2244(b)(1) by its terms governs state-prisoner habeas applications under §2254, and importing that relitigation bar into the distinct federal-prisoner scheme of §2255 improperly adds an extra, judge-made obstacle beyond Congress’s specific gatekeeping criteria in §2255(h), with severe real-world consequences for prisoners seeking to vindicate later-recognized constitutional rights. Given AEDPA’s already harsh timing regime (see §2255(f)(3) and Dodd v. United States), construing §2244(b)(1) to further foreclose merits review risks unjustly denying relief even where a claim becomes viable only after intervening Supreme Court decisions, contrary to fairness and access-to-justice values reflected in cases like Bousley and Reed. On jurisdiction, reading §2244(b)(3)(E) to strip this Court of certiorari review of §2255 authorization rulings would entrench circuit splits and create an accountability gap; Felker v. Turpin counsels against interpretations that unduly impair this Court’s essential role in supervising AEDPA’s gatekeeping regime. The better reading avoids both the overextension of §2244(b)(1) into §2255 and an expansive jurisdiction-stripping construction that would prevent this Court from correcting systemic errors.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 2244(b)(1) by its terms governs “a second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and importing that relitigation bar into the separate federal-prisoner scheme of §2255 adds a categorical limitation Congress did not place in §2255(h)’s expressly enumerated gatekeeping criteria. Reading AEDPA as a coherent whole, §2255(h) already supplies the workably administrable limits on successive federal motions, and the better textual inference is that Congress’s choice to specify §2254 in §2244(b)(1) was deliberate rather than an invitation to judicial supplementation. On the jurisdiction question, §2244(b)(3)(E) must be read narrowly as in Felker v. Turpin, which cautions against expansive constructions of “no review” provisions and confirms that AEDPA did not clearly eliminate all Supreme Court supervisory pathways; absent a clear statement, we should not assume Congress stripped certiorari jurisdiction to review §2255 authorization determinations. This reading preserves a workable mechanism for resolving acknowledged circuit splits without upsetting AEDPA’s finality aims, while leaving Congress free to speak more clearly if it wishes to foreclose certiorari in §2255 cases.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 2244(b)(1) by its terms governs “a second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and §2255 supplies its own, carefully enumerated gatekeeping rule in §2255(h); importing §2244(b)(1)’s categorical relitigation bar into §2255 adds an atextual restriction Congress did not place there. The separation-of-powers concern is acute in this context: when Congress specifies the conditions for reopening a federal judgment, courts may not append extra barriers in the name of “structure” or policy, especially where the plain language points the other way. As to §2244(b)(3)(E), Felker v. Turpin teaches that jurisdiction-stripping provisions should be read narrowly to avoid “troublesome” constitutional questions; at minimum, the provision should not be construed to foreclose this Court’s certiorari review of the antecedent legal question whether §2244(b)(1) applies to §2255 authorization decisions at all. Even if AEDPA can be harsh (see Dodd v. United States), that does not license courts to extend statutory bars beyond their text.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: AEDPA’s second-or-successive regime is an integrated framework in which §2255(h) expressly incorporates §2244’s authorization procedure, and reading §2244(b)(1)’s relitigation bar to apply in §2255 cases best fits AEDPA’s history, structure, and finality-focused purpose rather than creating a loophole for repeat federal collateral attacks. Practical workability and uniformity also favor that reading, because it prevents serial presentation of the same claim across multiple authorization attempts and aligns federal-prisoner practice with the analogous state-prisoner gatekeeping provisions. On jurisdiction, §2244(b)(3)(E)’s text plainly bars this Court from entertaining certiorari to review courts of appeals’ authorization decisions, and Felker v. Turpin upheld AEDPA’s limits by emphasizing that Congress can channel review while leaving other avenues (notably original habeas) available—avoiding an Article III conflict. While the resulting inability to resolve a split is a serious institutional concern (as noted in Avery and later statements), it is a problem for Congress to fix absent a clearer constitutional violation.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 2255(h) provides that a second-or-successive motion must be “certified as provided in section 2244,” which, read in context and according to its ordinary meaning, incorporates §2244(b)’s gatekeeping framework—including the relitigation bar in §2244(b)(1)—as part of the “requirements” for authorization. That structural reading accords with AEDPA’s design to restrict repetitive collateral attacks and with Felker v. Turpin’s description of §2244(b)(3) as the statute’s “gatekeeping” mechanism for second-or-successive applications. For the same reason, §2244(b)(3)(E)’s command that the authorization decision “shall not be appealable and shall not be the subject of a petition for a writ of certiorari” applies to those §2255 authorization determinations made “as provided in” §2244, even if that limits this Court’s usual certiorari review. Although the result can be harsh in some cases (cf. Dodd v. United States), that policy concern cannot overcome the text Congress chose.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 2244(b)(1) by its terms governs “a second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and importing that categorical relitigation bar into §2255 adds an extra restriction beyond Congress’s carefully specified gatekeeping criteria in §2255(h), raising serious procedural-fairness concerns for federal prisoners with later-arising Supreme Court claims. Reading AEDPA’s parallel schemes to preserve meaningful merits review when Congress has not clearly foreclosed it better fits the statute’s text and avoids the practical consequence of blocking potentially meritorious claims through an atextual overlay. On jurisdiction, §2244(b)(3)(E) expressly states that authorization decisions “shall not be … the subject of … a writ of certiorari,” and Felker v. Turpin recognizes Congress’s power to curtail certiorari review of gatekeeping determinations while leaving other avenues (e.g., the Court’s original habeas) untouched. Given that tension, the most faithful approach is to reject extending §2244(b)(1) to §2255, where the absence of clear text would otherwise combine with §2244(b)(3)(E)’s review bar to create an accountability gap and exacerbate circuit disparities.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether AEDPA’s claim-bar in 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners’ second-or-successive collateral attacks brought under 28 U.S.C. § 2255 (and, relatedly, whether 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(3)(E) prevents Supreme Court certiorari review of the court of appeals’ authorization decision).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(1), § 2244(b)(3)(E), and 28 U.S.C. § 2255 (including AEDPA’s second-or-successive framework and timing provisions such as § 2255(f)(3)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Bowe argues that § 2244(b)(1) by its text targets state-prisoner habeas petitions under § 2254 and therefore should not bar claims in a federal prisoner’s second-or-successive § 2255 motion; applying it to § 2255 improperly adds an extra, judge-made hurdle beyond what Congress specified for federal prisoners (who already must satisfy § 2255(h)’s gatekeeping), and the Court should resolve the acknowledged circuit split even if § 2244(b)(3)(E) is read to restrict ordinary certiorari review of authorization rulings.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States (and the court-appointed amicus supporting the judgment below on Question 1) contend that it is neither unfair nor unusual for AEDPA to prevent even diligent federal prisoners from benefiting from later legal changes, that AEDPA is designed to promote finality rather than repeated relitigation, and that applying § 2244(b)(1) to § 2255 motions is consistent with AEDPA’s overall second-or-successive scheme; they also invoke § 2244(b)(3)(E) as limiting Supreme Court review of authorization decisions, arguing the Court may lack certiorari jurisdiction over the court of appeals’ grant/denial of authorization.
key_precedents: Avery v. United States, 140 S. Ct. 1080 (2020) (Kavanaugh, J., statement respecting denial of certiorari)
In re Bowe, 144 S. Ct. 1170 (2024) (Sotomayor, J., statement respecting denial)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s textual argument that § 2244(b)(1) by its terms governs only an “application under section 2254” is the best point for the Petitioner, and I do not dismiss it; but I remain unpersuaded that we can treat AEDPA’s second-or-successive provisions as siloed when § 2255(h) expressly routes federal prisoners into § 2244’s gatekeeping architecture and Congress sought a coherent, finality-protecting scheme. Justice Thomas and Justice Kagan emphasize that importing § 2244(b)(1) would add a substantive restriction Congress did not write into § 2255(h), yet the cross-reference is to § 2244’s mechanism for managing successive filings, and reading it to exclude the basic “no re-presentation” rule risks an implausible gap that Congress is unlikely to have intended in an integrated regime. On the jurisdiction point raised by Justice Gorsuch and others, Felker still counsels restraint in expanding our review in this area; a minimalist course is to respect Congress’s channeling and apply AEDPA as a coordinated structure rather than creating atextual carve-outs to avoid a harder constitutional fight. Dodd, for me, reinforces that we apply AEDPA’s strict design as enacted even when consequences are harsh, and the Respondent’s reading better fits that structural design without inviting repetitive relitigation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s structural “integrated scheme” argument is the strongest on the other side, but under an originalist textual approach it cannot override Congress’s enacted limitation: § 2244(b)(1) by its terms governs only a “second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and a § 2255 motion is not that. As Justice Barrett notes, § 2255(h) separately and exhaustively enumerates the substantive limits for successive federal motions, and importing an additional § 2254-specific claim bar through a cross-reference to the authorization procedure would add a restriction Congress did not write. The Chief Justice’s reliance on Dodd does not move me because Dodd teaches fidelity to text even when harsh, not extending AEDPA’s harshness by inference. On the jurisdiction point raised by Justice Roberts, Felker counsels construing jurisdiction-stripping narrowly absent a clear statement, which supports reaching the statutory question without expanding § 2244(b)(1) beyond its terms.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s point that § 2244(b)(1) by its terms applies to an “application under section 2254” is the strongest textual argument for Petitioner, and I accept that the phrase cannot be ignored. But § 2255(h)’s express incorporation of § 2244’s authorization regime is best read as importing AEDPA’s integrated second-or-successive framework, including the baseline anti-relitigation rule of § 2244(b)(1); otherwise Congress would have created the anomalous gap the Chief Justice identifies, letting federal prisoners reassert the same claim repeatedly so long as they can squeeze through § 2255(h)’s gateway. Dodd supports applying AEDPA’s restrictive design as enacted even when it yields harsh results, and here the integrated-structure reading better reflects what Congress actually built than a hyper-literal, provision-isolated approach that undercuts finality. Felker, as Chief Justice Roberts notes, also counsels against carving out judge-made exceptions to Congress’s gatekeeping scheme based on speculative avoidance concerns.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point is the “integrated scheme” concern—reading § 2244(b)(1) as inapplicable to § 2255 could seem to create an anomalous gap and dilute finality. But that structural intuition cannot override Congress’s explicit line-drawing: § 2244(b)(1) by its terms governs only a “second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and importing it into § 2255 would add a third substantive hurdle beyond the two criteria Congress enacted in § 2255(h), not merely borrow § 2244(b)(3)’s authorization procedure as Justice Barrett explains. Dodd, invoked by Justice Alito, reinforces that we apply AEDPA as written even when outcomes are harsh—so we should not extend harshness by analogizing a § 2254-only claim bar to federal prisoners. On jurisdiction, Justice Kagan’s and Justice Gorsuch’s reading of Felker supports construing § 2244(b)(3)(E) narrowly enough to avoid insulating a recurring access-to-justice question from this Court’s review absent a clearer statement.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point is the “integrated scheme/anomalous gap” argument: that § 2255(h)’s routing through § 2244 implies importing § 2244(b)(1)’s claim bar to protect finality. But under a pragmatic textualist approach, that structural purpose cannot override Congress’s precise line-drawing—§ 2244(b)(1) expressly governs only “an application under section 2254,” while § 2255(h) separately and exhaustively states the substantive limits for successive federal motions, making the more natural reading that only § 2244(b)(3)’s authorization procedure is incorporated. Felker, invoked by Roberts, matters chiefly on the jurisdiction/avoidance question and pushes toward construing jurisdiction-stripping narrowly; it does not supply a basis to extend a § 2254-specific merits bar to § 2255 by implication. Administrability also favors this: courts can apply the clear, written division (2244(b)(1) for § 2254; § 2255(h) for § 2255) rather than litigate how much of § 2244 silently migrates across the cross-reference.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito’s harmonization argument is serious—AEDPA does pursue finality and § 2255(h) borrows § 2244’s authorization procedure—but under a textualist approach that structural aim cannot erase § 2244(b)(1)’s express limitation to “a…application under section 2254.” As Justice Barrett explains, Congress drafted distinct successive-motion limits for federal prisoners in § 2255(h); reading the cross-reference to import a § 2254-specific claim bar would add a substantive restriction Congress conspicuously did not include where it spelled out the exclusive criteria. Dodd, invoked by Roberts and Alito, strengthens rather than weakens this conclusion: it teaches we enforce AEDPA’s enacted lines even when harsh, not that we extend harshness by inference to cover a different statute. On jurisdiction, Felker supports construing § 2244(b)(3)(E) narrowly and cautions against treating it as a clear statement insulating an inapplicable statutory bar from this Court’s review.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s harmonization point—that § 2255(h)’s cross-reference to § 2244 implies importing § 2244(b)(1)’s claim-bar—is the best structural argument for Respondent, but under a precedent- and text-respecting approach it cannot override Congress’s explicit limitation of § 2244(b)(1) to an “application under section 2254.” As Justice Barrett emphasizes, § 2255(h) itself enumerates the substantive successive-motion limits for federal prisoners, and treating the cross-reference as silently adding a third restriction (a § 2254-specific claim bar) is an atextual expansion rather than faithful implementation. Dodd, invoked by Justice Alito, supports enforcing harsh statutes as written, not extending harshness by analogy beyond the enacted lines. On jurisdiction, Felker counsels narrow constructions of jurisdiction-stripping; that institutional and constitutional-avoidance backdrop reinforces deciding the merits by the statute’s clear textual boundary rather than entrenching a split through an expansive reading of the claim-bar.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito press the most serious point: § 2255(h)’s cross-reference to § 2244 reflects an integrated AEDPA scheme, and excluding § 2244(b)(1) arguably creates an “anomalous gap.” But under a textualist methodology, that structural intuition cannot override Congress’s express limitation of § 2244(b)(1) to a “second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” particularly when Congress separately set out the exclusive substantive limits for federal prisoners in § 2255(h). Dodd, invoked by Roberts and Alito, reinforces adherence to enacted lines—even when harsh—rather than extending a restriction Congress did not write for § 2255 movants. Felker bears on the jurisdictional question, but even if § 2244(b)(3)(E) is read to limit review of certain gatekeeping orders, that does not supply a warrant to broaden § 2244(b)(1) beyond its text to achieve perceived symmetry.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito’s strongest point is the structural one: § 2255(h)’s cross-reference to § 2244 suggests an integrated second-or-successive scheme aimed at finality, and reading § 2244(b)(1) out could create an “anomalous gap.” But that purposive harmonization cannot justify treating Congress’s limiting words—“an application under section 2254,” as Justice Barrett emphasizes—as surplusage, nor can it justify adding an extra substantive hurdle on top of the two criteria Congress expressly listed in § 2255(h). Dodd, invoked by Roberts/Alito, actually reinforces restraint: we enforce AEDPA’s harsh lines as written, rather than extending harshness by inference to a different statute Congress drafted separately. Felker, as Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh note, counsels narrow construction of jurisdiction-stripping and supports our addressing the statutory question on the merits rather than insulating a split behind a gatekeeping label.

John Roberts.reasoning: AEDPA’s second-or-successive framework is designed to promote finality and channel repeated collateral attacks through strict gatekeeping, and reading § 2244(b)(1)’s claim-bar as applicable in the § 2255 context best harmonizes the statute’s integrated scheme alongside § 2255(h)’s authorization requirements. On the Court’s ability to review the authorization ruling, § 2244(b)(3)(E) expressly withdraws certiorari jurisdiction over courts of appeals’ gatekeeping decisions, and Felker v. Turpin upheld AEDPA’s similar limitations while noting other potential avenues of review may remain, thereby avoiding a broader constitutional confrontation. Consistent with judicial minimalism and institutional legitimacy, the narrower course is to respect Congress’s jurisdictional and procedural choices in AEDPA rather than create an additional, court-crafted exception for § 2255 movants. This approach also accords with the Court’s general insistence on adhering to AEDPA’s text and structure even when it yields harsh results, as reflected in Dodd v. United States.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of § 2244(b)(1) expressly targets a "second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254," and a § 2255 motion is not an application under § 2254; reading § 2244(b)(1) to bar claims in § 2255 proceedings would depart from the statute’s ordinary meaning and improperly add to Congress’s distinct gatekeeping rule for federal prisoners in § 2255(h). AEDPA shows Congress knew how to speak separately to § 2254 and § 2255, and a textualist reading respects that structural choice rather than importing § 2254-specific claim bars into § 2255. As to review, Felker v. Turpin recognizes § 2244(b)(3)(E) as a restriction on certiorari review of gatekeeping decisions, but it also emphasizes that some avenues (including this Court’s original habeas) remained open; given the serious constitutional concerns if § 2244(b)(3)(E) were read to foreclose any meaningful Supreme Court supervision in this posture, the better reading is to decide the merits question without extending § 2244(b)(1) beyond its § 2254 text.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Although § 2244(b)(1) speaks in terms of a “habeas corpus application under section 2254,” AEDPA’s second-or-successive scheme is designed to impose stringent, uniform limits on repeat collateral attacks and to advance finality, and § 2255(h) expressly incorporates § 2244’s authorization procedure—strong evidence Congress expected § 2244(b)’s claim-bar to operate in this context as well. Reading § 2244(b)(1) to exclude § 2255 would create an anomalous gap allowing federal prisoners to relitigate previously presented claims despite AEDPA’s overall structure and purposes. This Court has already recognized that AEDPA can yield “harsh result[s]” for federal prisoners who seek to benefit from later legal developments, and it is not our role to soften that policy choice. Dodd v. United States, 545 U.S. 353, 359 (2005).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 2244(b)(1) by its terms governs a “habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and Congress separately specified the gatekeeping rules for federal prisoners’ second-or-successive collateral attacks in § 2255(h); importing § 2244(b)(1)’s additional claim-bar into § 2255 would add an extra obstacle beyond the text Congress enacted. Dodd v. United States underscores that AEDPA’s timing and successive-motion provisions already operate with severe practical consequences for federal prisoners under § 2255(f)(3) and § 2255(h), and those harsh results counsel against layering on a further, nontextual bar that predictably forecloses meritorious claims, particularly for prisoners with limited access to counsel and courts. Basic fairness principles recognized in cases like Bousley v. United States (permitting collateral review when a conviction rests on conduct not criminal under a later-corrected interpretation) reinforce the need to construe AEDPA’s limits as written, not expanded by analogy. Finally, § 2244(b)(3)(E) should not be read to insulate a circuit-split authorization regime from this Court’s review where the question is the meaning of federal statutes governing access to postconviction relief.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 2244(b)(1) by its terms bars claims in a “second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and Congress separately specified the gatekeeping criteria for federal prisoners in § 2255(h); importing § 2244(b)(1)’s additional claim-bar into § 2255 would add a restriction the text does not supply and would undermine statutory coherence. AEDPA’s structure reflects different pathways for state and federal prisoners, and the better workable reading is to apply § 2244(b)(1) where Congress said it applies while leaving § 2255(h) to do the limiting for federal prisoners (even if that means some later legal changes cannot be leveraged, as Dodd illustrates in a different timing context under § 2255(f)(3)). On the jurisdictional question, we should read § 2244(b)(3)(E)’s certiorari bar narrowly to avoid serious Exceptions Clause concerns and to preserve this Court’s ability to resolve the acknowledged circuit split, consistent with Felker’s caution against finding jurisdiction-stripping by implication. That approach respects finality while maintaining a workable, text-grounded system for second-or-successive review.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 2244(b)(1) by its plain terms governs a "second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254" and thus targets state-prisoner habeas, not federal prisoners’ motions under § 2255; importing that claim-bar into § 2255 adds a restriction Congress did not write, beyond the gatekeeping Congress did enact in § 2255(h). Reading the statute as written also respects separation of powers by leaving any additional limits on federal prisoners’ successive collateral review to Congress, not courts. As for § 2244(b)(3)(E), Felker recognizes Congress curtailed certiorari review of gatekeeping rulings, but it also teaches we should construe jurisdiction-stripping provisions narrowly and not assume they foreclose this Court’s ability to correct an inferior court’s application of an inapplicable legal requirement. On this textual and structural reading, § 2244(b)(1) does not bar Bowe’s § 2255 claim, and § 2244(b)(3)(E) does not defeat review at least where the court of appeals’ disposition rests on a legally erroneous jurisdictional premise rather than a merits gatekeeping "grant or denial" within the statute.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 2244(b)(1) by its text applies to “a second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and Congress separately specified the gatekeeping limits for federal prisoners in § 2255(h); reading § 2244(b)(1) to add a further claim-bar to § 2255 motions is hard to reconcile with that structure and exceeds what Congress enacted. On jurisdiction, Felker v. Turpin construed § 2244(b)(3)(E)’s certiorari bar in light of remaining Supreme Court review avenues (original habeas), and Justice Souter’s concurrence warned the Exceptions Clause issue would be “open” if other avenues closed; after decisions narrowing alternative paths for federal prisoners, a narrow construction of § 2244(b)(3)(E) that preserves certiorari review here avoids serious constitutional doubt. That interpretation also promotes practical workability by allowing this Court to resolve the entrenched circuit split over whether § 2244(b)(1) governs § 2255, rather than entrenching divergent rules for similarly situated federal prisoners. Given AEDPA’s emphasis on clear, administrable gatekeeping rules, the better reading is to apply the limits Congress expressly placed in § 2255(h) and not import § 2244(b)(1)’s distinct claim-bar from the § 2254 context.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of § 2244(b)(1) expressly bars claims only in a “second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and a § 2255 motion is not such an application; reading § 2255(h)’s cross-reference to silently import § 2244(b)(1)’s § 2254-specific claim bar would depart from AEDPA’s carefully drafted, provision-by-provision scheme for federal prisoners. The better textual reading is that § 2255(h) incorporates the gatekeeping mechanism in § 2244(b)(3) (authorization procedures) but does not transform § 2244(b)(1)’s state-prisoner claim bar into an additional limitation on federal prisoners beyond the two criteria Congress listed in § 2255(h). Likewise, § 2244(b)(3)(E)’s “shall not be appealable” clause, as construed in Felker v. Turpin, does not clearly strip this Court’s certiorari jurisdiction over a § 2255 authorization decision absent an unmistakable statement, and jurisdiction-stripping is strictly construed. Given AEDPA’s textual precision and this Court’s reluctance to extend habeas restrictions beyond their terms (cf. Dodd v. United States’ adherence to statutory text even when harsh), I would reverse.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The text and structure of AEDPA indicate that § 2244(b)(1)’s claim-bar targets state-prisoner habeas petitions under § 2254, while Congress separately and specifically prescribed the gatekeeping limits for federal prisoners in § 2255(h); importing § 2244(b)(1) into § 2255 adds a further procedural hurdle not clearly enacted for federal prisoners. Given the serious practical consequences for procedural fairness—especially where new rules may arise after a first collateral attack—finality concerns cannot justify extending an unambiguous state-habeas bar to federal prisoners absent a clear statement. On the jurisdictional issue, Felker v. Turpin counsels narrow readings of jurisdiction-stripping and cautions against implied repeals, supporting construing § 2244(b)(3)(E) not to foreclose this Court’s review where otherwise the Court would be unable to resolve an acknowledged circuit split. This interpretation avoids grave constitutional questions about Congress’s power to eliminate Supreme Court oversight while ensuring a workable, uniform federal postconviction regime.
